name: Luvian / HLuvian
catalog_citation: Melchert, H. Craig. 2004. "Luvian." In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages, 576-584. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. (Reprinted 2008 as "Luvian" in Woodard (ed.), The Ancient Languages of Asia Minor, 31-3…
catalog_locator: p. 580, sec. 3.2 Vowels (Phonology). Image-only author scan held at, PDF p. 31; running head "LUVIAN 579" on PDF p. 3…
catalog_quote: Luvian has only three vowels, /a/, /i/, and /u/, in contrasting short and long varieties. While there are some underlying long vowels, most phonetic length is due to synchronic rules which lengthen underlying short vowels under the accent: contrast sentence-initial conjunction pā < /pá/ versus enclitic -pa < /-pa/, or adverb ānnan "under" < /ánnan/ versus annān pātanza "under the feet" < /annán/ with accent shift in a prepositional phrase (see Melchert 1994a:247 for further discussion). ... Certain facts about the placement of the accent may be inferred from the prehistoric and synchronic rules cited in the preceding two paragraphs, but the evidence is limited, and the risk of circularity of argument is high.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.citation: Melchert, H. Craig. 2004. "Luvian." In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages, 576-584. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. (Reprinted as Melchert 2008, "Luvian", in Woodard (ed.), The Ancient Languages of Asia Minor, 31-39; Glottolog ref 104631.)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (image-only scan, Acrobat Paper Capture; no usable text layer) via the held 300-dpi scanned cune1239/scanned/ and viewed the page crop cune1239/scanned/ directly. The quoted passage is on the image verbatim under the heading "3.2 Vowels": "While there are some underlying long vowels, most phonetic length is due to synchronic rules which lengthen underlying short vowels under the accent: contrast sentence-initial conjunction pā < /pá/ versus enclitic -pa < /-pa/, or adverb ānnan "under" < /ánnan/ versus annān pātanza "under the feet" < /annán/ with accent shift in a prepositional phrase (see Melchert 1994a:247 for further discussion)." and, after the diphthong sentences, "Certain fact…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Luwian (in both scripts) had a word accent with a strong stress component that lengthened accented short vowels (in open syllables) and conditioned consonant lenition, but its position is not directly written and cannot be stated as a rule: the placement is only inferred word by word from lengthening/plene and lenition effects, with high risk of circularity (Melchert 2004); 'the synchronic nature of stress in Luwian is unclear' (Yakubovich 2013: 115). The inferred system is an inherited, non-fixed (lexically/morphologically determined) accent: it differs between full words and enclitics, shifts within a prepositional phrase (ānnan vs annān pātanza), and shows radical vs suffixal accent in different verb classes (Vertegaal 2018: 172). The nearest positive catalog class would be lexical (unpredictable), but no source asserts that.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics are unaccented (Melchert 2004; Yakubovich 2013; Vertegaal 2018: 165 fn. 5, 174); accent shift in prepositional phrases (Melchert 2004: 580); possible clitic-induced accent shift before =ha discussed and left open (Vertegaal 2018: 193).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Melchert's pā/-pa and ānnan/annān pātanza contrast is between orthotonic word, enclitic, and phrase-internal (prepositional-phrase) accentuation. Extinct written language (c. 1400-700 BCE); the script writes no accent; 'accents' in transliteration (sá, sà) are homophone indices, not prosody (Payne 2010: 13; Kammenhuber 1969: 152 n. 1; Werner 1991: 16).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Melchert 2004 'Luvian') describes Luvian as one language written in two scripts and does not separate Cuneiform Luvian (cune1239) from Hieroglyphic Luvian (hier1240); the p. 580 accent statement is not script-specific, and the same passage is the statement already held for cune1239 (its scanned and crop live in that folder). The Hieroglyphic-Luwian-specific literature opened (Vertegaal 2017, 2018, 2020) agrees: HLuw. words other than clitics were accented, plene spelling marks length not accent, and accent position is only inferable form by form. Extinct language, TR/SY, c. 1400-700 BCE.
